PAX6 is the master control gene for the entire eye development process; its haploinsufficiency or mutation is the classic cause of aniridia.
MSX1 is involved in tooth development and cleft palate, not the primary regulation of iris formation.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 485 (Book Page): PAX6 is the key regulatory gene for eye development... Mutations in PAX6 result in aniridia and may also contribute to anophthalmia and microphthalmia.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
statement: A patient presents with increased intraocular pressure (glaucoma) due to a congenital blockage in the drainage of aqueous humor. In the developing eye, where is this fluid normally resorbed into the bloodstream after circulating through the anterior chamber?
options: The intraretinal space between the retinal layers
The iridopupillary membrane
The scleral venous sinus at the iridocorneal angle
The hyaloid canal within the vitreous body
The ciliary process of the ciliary body
correctOption: The scleral venous sinus at the iridocorneal angle
optionExplanations: The intraretinal space is a transient embryonic space between the pigmented and neural layers of the retina that normally disappears as they appose.
The iridopupillary membrane is a transient mesenchymal layer in front of the lens that must disappear to allow light to enter; it is not a drainage site.
The canal of Schlemm (scleral venous sinus) is the primary exit for aqueous humor; its blockage or malformation leads to increased intraocular pressure.
The hyaloid canal is a remnant of the hyaloid artery path within the vitreous; it does not serve as a drainage pathway for aqueous humor.
The ciliary processes are the site of aqueous humor production, not resorption; production occurs in the posterior chamber.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 484 (Book Page): From the anterior chamber, the fluid passes through the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm) at the iridocorneal angle where it is resorbed into the bloodstream.

category: Describe the development of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses
statement: During the sixth week of gestation, the nasal pits undergo significant deepening. Which physiological event initially separates these primitive nasal chambers from the oral cavity before the formation of the secondary palate?
options: Formation of the oronasal membrane
Descent of the nasal septum
Canalization of the nasolacrimal duct
Merging of the medial nasal prominences
Fusion of the palatine shelves
correctOption: Formation of the oronasal membrane
optionExplanations: The oronasal membrane is a transient structure that separates the deepening nasal pits from the primitive oral cavity before it eventually breaks down.
The nasal septum grows downward to join the newly formed palate later in development; it is not the initial separating structure.
The nasolacrimal duct is involved in drainage from the eye to the inferior meatus and does not act as a partition between the nose and mouth.
Merging of the medial nasal prominences forms the intermaxillary segment and primary palate, but the depth of the cavity is initially blocked by the oronasal membrane.
The fusion of palatine shelves occurs later (7th-10th week) to form the secondary palate, which creates the definitive separation.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 422 (Book Page): At first, the oronasal membrane separates the pits from the primitive oral cavity by way of the newly formed foramina, the primitive choanae (Fig. 17.31C).

category: Describe the development of face and nasolacrimal duct and their respective congenital anomalies
statement: Upon completion of its development, the nasolacrimal duct establishes a permanent drainage pathway into which anatomical location?
options: Nasopharynx directly via the auditory tube
Middle meatus of the nasal cavity
Superior meatus of the nasal cavity
Inferior meatus of the nasal cavity
Oropharynx
correctOption: Inferior meatus of the nasal cavity
optionExplanations: The auditory tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx; it is not the drainage site for the nasolacrimal system.
The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior/middle ethmoidal sinuses.
The superior meatus receives drainage from the posterior ethmoidal air cells, not the nasolacrimal duct.
The nasolacrimal duct specifically drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the inferior meatus, located under the inferior nasal concha.
The oropharynx is posterior to the oral cavity and does not receive the nasolacrimal duct.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 420 (Book Page): The nasolacrimal duct then runs from the medial corner of the eye to the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity

category: Describe the development and histogenesis of auditory tube, tympanic cavity, tonsils, thymus and parathyroid
statement: The development of the thymus is unique among the pharyngeal pouch derivatives because it undergoes significant changes in size and composition across the lifespan. Which physiological description best characterizes the thymus in an older adult compared to a young child?
options: It migrates back toward the pharyngeal region.
It undergoes calcification to form the thymic bone.
It is replaced by highly vascularized lymphoid follicles.
It continues to grow and expand until the sixth decade.
It is atrophied and largely replaced by fatty tissue.
correctOption: It is atrophied and largely replaced by fatty tissue.
optionExplanations: The thymus does not migrate postnatally; its anatomical position in the anterior mediastinum is fixed after development.
There is no such structure as 'thymic bone'; the thymus remains a soft-tissue organ until it involutes.
While the thymus is a lymphoid organ, in the elderly, it loses its lymphoid density and becomes predominantly adipose.
Thymic growth ceases at puberty, after which it begins the process of involution.
Involution is the standard physiological process where thymic tissue is replaced by fat following puberty.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 411 (Book Page): Growth and development of the thymus continue until puberty. In the young child, the thymus occupies considerable space in the thorax... In older persons, it is difficult to recognize because it is atrophied and replaced by fatty tissue.

category: Describe the development of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses
statement: In the development of the paranasal sinuses, these structures appear as diverticula of the lateral nasal wall. When do they typically achieve their maximum size, influencing the definitive shape of the adult face?
options: At the onset of the deciduous tooth eruption
Immediately following the first breath at birth
By the end of the second year of postnatal life
During the seventh month of intrauterine life
During the period of puberty
correctOption: During the period of puberty
optionExplanations: Deciduous teeth erupting (6–24 months) correlates with some facial growth, but sinus expansion peaks much later.
At birth, the paranasal sinuses are rudimentary or virtually absent, contributing to the small appearance of the newborn's face.
The second year marks the closure of the anterior fontanelle, but the sinuses continue to expand well into the first decade and beyond.
While some sinuses start developing in utero, they are far from their maximum size in the seventh month.
The significant facial changes seen during puberty are largely due to the final expansion of the paranasal sinuses and the growth of the jaws to accommodate permanent teeth.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 422 (Book Page): Paranasal air sinuses develop as diverticula of the lateral nasal wall... They reach their maximum size during puberty and contribute to the definitive shape of the face.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: Molecular regulation of skull development involves precise signaling at the neural crest-mesoderm boundaries. Which ligand-receptor interaction is specifically identified as providing an 'anti-adhesive' or repelling activity to prevent the premature closure of cranial sutures?
options: SHH and PTCH1
Ephrin-B1 and EphB
BMP7 and BMPR2
MSX2 and TWIST1
FGF8 and FGFR1
correctOption: Ephrin-B1 and EphB
optionExplanations: Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) establishes the midline of the face and inhibits PAX6, but its role in the cranial sutures is secondary to Ephrins and FGFs.
Ephrin-B1 (encoded by EFNB1) acts on EphB receptors to mediate cell repulsion at boundaries. Mutations here lead to craniofrontonasal syndrome via premature fusion.
BMP signaling is critical for bone induction and patterning in the facial prominences but is not the primary 'repellent' signal described for suture patency.
MSX2 and TWIST1 are transcription factors that regulate neural crest proliferation in the frontal bones, but they are not the ligands/receptors mediating cell repulsion.
FGF/FGFR signaling is primarily involved in regulating cell proliferation and osteogenic differentiation, rather than providing the repellent anti-adhesive force.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): EFNB1 encodes ephrin-B1, a ligand for EphB receptors that causes cells to repel each other, a kind of antiadhesive activity and important for preventing premature suture closure.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
statement: Initially, the inner and outer layers of the optic cup are separated by a space which subsequently disappears as the two layers appose each other. What is this transient space called?
options: Anterior chamber
Scleral venous sinus
Intraretinal space
Hyaloid canal
Pharyngeal cleft
correctOption: Intraretinal space
optionExplanations: The anterior chamber is a space formed by vacuolization in the mesenchyme between the lens/iris and the cornea.
The scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm) is a drainage channel for aqueous humor at the iridocorneal angle.
The intraretinal space is the lumen between the inner (neural) and outer (pigmented) layers of the optic cup. Its persistence can lead to congenital retinal detachment.
The hyaloid canal is a remnant in the vitreous body after the hyaloid artery disappears, not the space between retinal layers.
Pharyngeal clefts are external grooves between pharyngeal arches in the neck region, completely unrelated to eye development.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 481 (Book Page): The inner and outer layers of this cup are initially separated by a lumen, the intraretinal space (Fig. 20.2B), but soon this lumen disappears, and the two layers appose each other (Fig. 20.2D,E).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Differentiation of the Otic Vesicle Components
statement: During the morphological differentiation of the otocyst, which specific combination of structures is entirely derived from the dorsal component of the auditory vesicle?
options: Spiral organ of Corti and ductus reuniens
Statoacoustic ganglion and spiral limbus
Cochlear duct and saccule
Utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic duct
Scala vestibuli and scala tympani
correctOption: Utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic duct
optionExplanations: The spiral organ of Corti develops from the cochlear duct, which is a ventral derivative, and the ductus reuniens is the persisting narrow connection between the saccule and cochlear duct.
The statoacoustic ganglion is formed by cells breaking away from the otocyst wall combined with neural crest cells, while the spiral limbus is a ridge formed within the cochlear duct.
The cochlear duct and saccule are derivatives of the ventral component of the otocyst, not the dorsal part.
The dorsal component of the auditory vesicle (otocyst) specifically differentiates into the utricle, the three semicircular canals, and the endolymphatic duct.
The scala vestibuli and scala tympani are perilymphatic spaces formed by the vacuolization of the surrounding mesenchyme/cartilage, not from the epithelial otocyst itself.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 471 (Book Page): During later development, each vesicle divides into (1) a ventral component that gives rise to the saccule and cochlear duct and (2) a dorsal component that forms the utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic duct (Figs. 19.3, 19.4, 19.5, and 19.6).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
statement: Which clinical condition is specifically characterized by a complete absence of the iris, often resulting from a mutation in the PAX6 master regulatory gene?
options: Microphthalmia
Aphakia
Cyclopia
Glaucoma
Aniridia
correctOption: Aniridia
optionExplanations: Microphthalmia describes an eye that is too small, which can have various genetic and environmental causes, including PAX6, but is not specifically the absence of the iris.
Aphakia refers to the absence of the lens, which is an inductive failure of the surface ectoderm.
Cyclopia involves a single median eye due to midline defects, which is a more global failure of the eye field to separate.
Glaucoma is a condition of increased intraocular pressure, often due to blockage of the canal of Schlemm, rather than a congenital absence of a structure.
Aniridia is the complete absence of the iris, classically linked to mutations in the PAX6 gene which regulates the development of the distal optic cup.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 488 (Book Page): Congenital aphakia [absence of the lens] and aniridia [absence of the iris; Fig. 20.11] are rare anomalies that result from disturbances in induction... Mutations in PAX6 result in aniridia.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
statement: The optic stalk undergoes a significant transformation to become the optic nerve. Which structure, originally located in the choroid fissure, eventually resides in the center of the optic nerve?
options: Statoacoustic ganglion
Central artery of the retina
Endolymphatic duct
Primary vitreous body
Optic vesicle lumen
correctOption: Central artery of the retina
optionExplanations: The statoacoustic ganglion is associated with the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), not the optic nerve.

The hyaloid artery enters the optic cup via the choroid fissure of the optic stalk. When the fissure closes, the artery is trapped in the center of the developing optic nerve, becoming the central artery of the retina.
The endolymphatic duct is a derivative of the otic vesicle (ear), not the eye.
The vitreous body occupies the posterior chamber of the eye, not the lumen of the optic nerve.
The optic vesicle lumen (intraretinal space) disappears as the layers appose; it does not form the center of the nerve.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 485 (Book Page): The optic stalk is thus transformed into the optic nerve. Its center contains a portion of the hyaloid artery, later called the central artery of the retina.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
statement: During the histogenesis of the internal ear, the cochlear duct (scala media) is separated from the scala tympani by which specialized structure?
options: Spiral limbus
Basilar membrane
Spiral ligament
Tectorial membrane
Vestibular membrane
correctOption: Basilar membrane
optionExplanations: The spiral limbus is derived from the inner ridge of the cochlear duct and serves as the attachment point for the tectorial membrane.
The basilar membrane serves as the structural floor of the cochlear duct, separating it from the scala tympani.
The spiral ligament attaches the lateral wall of the cochlear duct to the surrounding cartilaginous shell.
The tectorial membrane is a gelatinous structure within the cochlear duct that covers the hair cells; it is not a boundary between the scalas.
The vestibular membrane separates the cochlear duct from the scala vestibuli, not the scala tympani.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 472 (Book Page): The cochlear duct is then separated from the scala vestibuli by the vestibular membrane and from the scala tympani by the basilar membrane (Fig. 19.4C).

category: Describe the development of pharyngeal arches, grooves, pouches and membrane and give derivatives and fate of each of them
coreConcept: Basic Structural Components of Pharyngeal Arches
statement: Each pharyngeal arch is characterized by a specific set of developmental components. According to the structural organization of these arches, which of the following represents the standard constituent elements found within the mesenchymal core of a typical pharyngeal arch?
options: A vein, a spinal nerve, a ligamentous primordium, and an endocrine bud
A venous sinus, a cranial nerve, a cartilage rod, and an ectodermal placode
An artery, a sensory ganglion, a respiratory bud, and a neural crest stream
An artery, a lymphatic vessel, a smooth muscle layer, and a dermal plate
An artery, a cranial nerve, a muscular element, and a skeletal bar
correctOption: An artery, a cranial nerve, a muscular element, and a skeletal bar
optionExplanations: Pharyngeal arches are supplied by cranial nerves, not spinal nerves, and contain specific skeletal elements rather than general endocrine buds.
While arches contain cartilage, they are defined by their arterial components (aortic arches) rather than venous sinuses, and ectodermal placodes are external to the mesenchymal core.
Neural crest cells contribute to the mesenchyme of the arch, but the formal components of an arch are listed as the artery, nerve, muscle, and skeletal element.
The muscular element of the pharyngeal arch is skeletal/branchiomeric muscle, not smooth muscle, and the focus is on the cartilaginous bar rather than a dermal plate.

Every pharyngeal arch contains four essential components: a specific aortic arch (artery), a specific cranial nerve that supplies the derivatives of that arch, a myogenic core that forms specific muscles, and a cartilaginous/skeletal rod that provides the framework.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 406 (Book Page): Each pharyngeal arch consists of a core of mesenchymal tissue covered on the outside by surface ectoderm and on the inside by epithelium of endodermal origin... each pharyngeal arch is characterized by its own muscular components. The muscular components of each arch have their own cranial nerve... In addition, each arch has its own arterial component.

category: Describe the development of pharyngeal arches, grooves, pouches and membrane and give derivatives and fate of each of them
statement: During the development of the hyoid bone, different pharyngeal arches contribute to its various components. Which structure is a skeletal derivative of the second pharyngeal arch?
options: Thyroid cartilage
Greater horn of the hyoid bone
Lower portion of the body of the hyoid bone
Sphenomandibular ligament
Lesser horn of the hyoid bone
correctOption: Lesser horn of the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The thyroid cartilage is formed by the fusion of the cartilaginous components of the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches.
The greater horn of the hyoid is a derivative of the third pharyngeal arch, not the second.
The lower portion of the hyoid body is also derived from the third pharyngeal arch.
The sphenomandibular ligament is a remnant of Meckel's cartilage from the first pharyngeal arch.
The second arch (Reichert's cartilage) forms the lesser horn and the upper part of the hyoid body.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 390 (Book Page): The cartilage of the second or hyoid arch (Reichert cartilage)... gives rise to the stapes, styloid process... lesser horn and upper part of the body of the hyoid bone.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
statement: Which developmental defect is characterized by a cleft in the iris, often extending into the ciliary body and retina, due to the failure of the choroid fissure to close?
options: Cyclopia
Microphthalmia
Aphakia
Aniridia
Coloboma
correctOption: Coloboma
optionExplanations: Cyclopia is a midline defect where the eyes are fused into a single unit, usually associated with holoprosencephaly.
Microphthalmia is a condition where the eye is abnormally small, usually due to intrauterine infections or genetic factors.
Aphakia refers to the congenital absence of the lens, typically due to failure of lens induction.
Aniridia is the complete absence of the iris, often linked to PAX6 mutations, rather than a specific cleft from fissure failure.
Coloboma results specifically from the failure of the choroid fissure to fuse during the 7th week of development, leaving a gap or cleft in ocular structures.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 487 (Book Page): Coloboma may occur if the choroid fissure fails to close. Normally, this fissure closes during the seventh week of development... a cleft persists... usually in the iris only—coloboma iridis.

category: Describe the development of larynx
coreConcept: Molecular Induction of the Respiratory Diverticulum
statement: In the signaling cascade for respiratory development, what is the specific role of Retinoic Acid (RA) in the induction of the larynx and lower respiratory structures?
options: It inhibits the expression of SHH to allow for bilateral lung bud separation
It promotes the apoptosis of the tracheoesophageal ridges
It causes upregulation of the transcription factor TBX4 in the gut endoderm
It maintains the patency of the laryngeal orifice through BMP4 suppression
It acts as a primary morphogen to induce FGF8 in the second pharyngeal pouch
correctOption: It causes upregulation of the transcription factor TBX4 in the gut endoderm
optionExplanations: SHH is involved in midline establishment but its primary interaction with RA in this specific context is not the separation of lung buds.
RA does not promote apoptosis of the ridges; the ridges fuse to form the septum, a process involving epithelial-mesenchymal signaling.
Retinoic acid produced by adjacent mesoderm triggers the expression of TBX4 in the foregut endoderm, which is the master signal for the formation of the respiratory diverticulum.
BMP4 is involved in the molecular patterning of the lung buds, but RA's first identified step is the induction of TBX4 at the diverticulum site.
FGF8 is expressed in the anterior endoderm of pharyngeal pouches, but RA's primary respiratory role is via TBX4 in the foregut endoderm.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 343 (Book Page): This increase in RA causes upregulation of the transcription factor TBX4 expressed in the endoderm of the gut tube at the site of the respiratory diverticulum. TBX4 induces formation of the bud and the continued growth and differentiation of the lungs.

category: Describe the development of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses
statement: In the development of the nasal passages, a transition occurs from primitive to definitive choanae. Where are the definitive choanae located following the completion of the secondary palate?
options: Within the substance of the lateral nasal wall
At the level of the incisive foramen
Immediately behind the primary palate
At the junction of the nasal cavity and the pharynx
At the floor of the nasolacrimal groove
correctOption: At the junction of the nasal cavity and the pharynx
optionExplanations: The lateral nasal wall is where paranasal sinuses develop as diverticula, not the location of the choanae.
The incisive foramen is the midline landmark between the primary and secondary palates, not the site of the definitive choanae.
The primitive choanae are located immediately behind the primary palate; the definitive ones are much further posterior.
Definitive choanae are established once the secondary palate is complete, marking the posterior boundary where the nasal cavity opens into the nasopharynx.
The nasolacrimal groove is located externally between the maxillary and lateral nasal prominences and is unrelated to the choanae.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 422 (Book Page): Later, with formation of the secondary palate and further development of the primitive nasal chambers (Fig. 17.31D), the definitive choanae lie at the junction of the nasal cavity and the pharynx.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the clinic with an abnormally long and narrow skull. Physical examination reveals prominent frontal and occipital bossing. Radiographic imaging confirms the premature closure of a single suture. Which suture and associated clinical condition are most likely present?
options: Coronal suture; Brachycephaly
Lambdoid suture; Plagiocephaly
Metopic suture; Trigonocephaly
Sagittal suture; Scaphocephaly
All sutures; Kleeblattschadel
correctOption: Sagittal suture; Scaphocephaly
optionExplanations: Premature closure of the coronal sutures (bilaterally) results in a short, broad skull known as brachycephaly, not a long/narrow one.
Plagiocephaly typically refers to asymmetric flattening, often from unilateral coronal or lambdoid suture closure, rather than symmetrical elongation.
Metopic suture closure results in a triangular forehead (trigonocephaly), which is not described by prominent frontal and occipital bossing with elongation.
Correct. Scaphocephaly is caused by the premature closure of the sagittal suture, preventing lateral growth and forcing the brain to expand the skull in the anterior-posterior direction.
Kleeblattschadel (cloverleaf skull) involves the premature closure of all or most sutures, resulting in a trilobed appearance, not just a long/narrow shape.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): Early closure of the sagittal suture [57% of cases] results in frontal and occipital expansion, and the skull becomes long and narrow [scaphocephaly] [Fig. 10.9].

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: In the context of tracheoesophageal fistulas (TEFs), which physiological mechanism best explains the frequent occurrence of polyhydramnios in the mother during the third trimester?
options: Overproduction of fetal lung fluid by the respiratory diverticulum
Impaired maternal resorption of fluid across the placental membrane
Reflux of gastric contents into the amniotic sac via the fistula
Excessive fetal urination due to renal agenesis associated with VACTERL
Failure of the fetus to swallow and pass amniotic fluid to the gastrointestinal tract
correctOption: Failure of the fetus to swallow and pass amniotic fluid to the gastrointestinal tract
optionExplanations: Lung fluid production is a normal process, but its overproduction is not the primary driver for polyhydramnios in esophageal/tracheal defects.
Polyhydramnios in TEF is a fetal-driven mechanical issue related to fluid cycling, not a primary defect in maternal placental resorption physiology.
While gastric contents can enter the trachea through a fistula, the primary cause of excess amniotic volume is the mechanical inability to route swallowed fluid to the gut.
Renal agenesis, part of the VACTERL association, actually leads to oligohydramnios (insufficient fluid) because the fetal urine is a primary source of amniotic fluid.
Normal amniotic fluid volume is maintained by fetal swallowing and intestinal absorption; in esophageal atresia (often seen with TEF), this cycle is broken, leading to fluid accumulation.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 345 (Book Page): A complication of some TEFs is polyhydramnios because in some types of TEF, amniotic fluid, when swallowed, does not pass to the stomach and intestines.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
statement: Exposure to which teratogen during the critical period of facial development (weeks 4-7) is most strongly associated with an increased risk of orofacial clefts, specifically affecting the fusion of the lip and palate?
options: Heparin
Tetracycline
Valproic acid
Streptomycin
Penicillin
correctOption: Valproic acid
optionExplanations: Heparin does not cross the placenta and is not associated with structural congenital malformations like cleft lip.
Tetracycline is primarily associated with the discoloration of teeth and hypoplasia of enamel, not the structural fusion failures of the lip.
Valproic acid, an anticonvulsant, is a known teratogen that disrupts the signaling required for facial prominence fusion, leading to cleft lip and palate.
Streptomycin is associated with vestibulocochlear nerve damage (cranial nerve VIII) and ototoxicity, not facial clefting.
Penicillin is generally considered safe during pregnancy and is not linked to the pathogenesis of orofacial clefts.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 428 (Book Page): Other cases are caused by exposure to teratogenic compounds, such as anticonvulsant medications, particularly valproic acid.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
statement: In the developing internal ear, the ductus reuniens serves as a critical anatomical landmark. What does this structure connect?
options: Saccule and cochlear duct
Middle ear and nasopharynx
Scala vestibuli and scala tympani
Utricle and semicircular canals
Endolymphatic duct and endolymphatic sac
correctOption: Saccule and cochlear duct
optionExplanations: The ductus reuniens is the small, constricted epithelial tube that maintains the connection between the saccule and the cochlear duct.
The connection between the middle ear (tympanic cavity) and the nasopharynx is the auditory (eustachian) tube.
The scala vestibuli and scala tympani are connected at the apex of the cochlea via the helicotrema, not the ductus reuniens.
The utricle and semicircular canals are connected directly; they are part of the dorsal component of the otic vesicle.
The endolymphatic duct leads to the endolymphatic sac, but this connection is not termed the ductus reuniens.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 472 (Book Page): A connection between the cochlear duct and the remaining portion of the saccule is maintained but confined to a narrow pathway, the ductus reuniens (Fig. 19.3E; see also Fig. 19.8).

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: A neonate is born with severe limb shortening and a 'cloverleaf' skull (kleeblattschadel). Radiographic imaging shows relatively long, straight femurs. Which genetic condition and receptor mutation are most consistent with this specific phenotype?
options: Thanatophoric dysplasia Type II; mutation in FGFR3.
Boston-type craniosynostosis; mutation in TWIST1.
Thanatophoric dysplasia Type I; mutation in FGFR2.
Achondroplasia; mutation in FGFR1.
Cleidocranial dysostosis; mutation in MSX2.
correctOption: Thanatophoric dysplasia Type II; mutation in FGFR3.
optionExplanations: Type II Thanatophoric dysplasia is specifically identified by the kleeblattschadel (cloverleaf skull) and relatively long, straight femurs, caused by constitutive activation of FGFR3.
Boston-type is a craniosynostosis caused by MSX2 mutations, while Saethre-Chotzen is caused by TWIST1; neither is the primary cause of thanatophoric cloverleaf skull.
Thanatophoric dysplasia Type I is characterized by curved, short femurs ('telephone receiver' femurs), distinct from the straight femurs of Type II.
Achondroplasia involves FGFR3 mutations but is usually not neonatal lethal and typically does not present with a cloverleaf skull.
Cleidocranial dysostosis involves delayed closure of sutures and missing clavicles, not premature closure leading to a cloverleaf skull.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): Thanatophoric dysplasia is the most common neonatal lethal form... type II individuals have straight, relatively long femurs and severe cloverleaf skull caused by craniosynostosis (Fig. 10.12). ...Common to all of these forms of skeletal dysplasias are mutations in FGFR3.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: Postnatal growth of the flat bones of the skull vault is a dynamic process that allows the skull to expand in tandem with the brain. Which physiological mechanism best explains how these bones increase in size while maintaining their relative thickness?
options: Expansion of the paranasal air sinuses pushing the plates outward
Apposition of new layers on the outer surface with internal osteoclastic resorption
Fusion of bone spicules at the sutures followed by chondrocyte hypertrophy
Endochondral replacement of the fontanelles
Interstitial growth within the primary ossification center
correctOption: Apposition of new layers on the outer surface with internal osteoclastic resorption
optionExplanations: While air sinuses do enlarge during puberty and influence facial shape, they are not the mechanism for the growth of the flat bones of the neurocranium vault.
Skull vault bones enlarge through a coordinated loop: osteoblasts deposit new bone on the external (outer) surface, while osteoclasts resorb bone from the internal (inner) surface.
Bone spicules do radiate from primary centers, but they do not involve chondrocyte hypertrophy, as these are membranous bones, not cartilaginous ones.
The fontanelles are membranous (connective tissue) and are replaced by bone via intramembranous ossification, not endochondral ossification.
Interstitial growth is characteristic of cartilage, not bone, as bone can only grow by apposition due to its rigid calcified matrix.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 269 (Book Page): With further growth during fetal and postnatal life, membranous bones enlarge by apposition of new layers on the outer surface and by simultaneous osteoclastic resorption from the inside.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
statement: A condition characterized by the presence of a small eyeball, often only two-thirds of the normal volume, is frequently associated with intrauterine infections such as toxoplasmosis. What is the correct clinical term for this anomaly?
options: Cyclopia
Microphthalmia
Anophthalmia
Synophthalmia
Aphakia
correctOption: Microphthalmia
optionExplanations: Cyclopia is the presence of a single median eye, a severe midline defect.
Microphthalmia is defined as a abnormally small eye, often resulting from developmental arrest or infection-induced damage during organogenesis.
Anophthalmia refers to the complete absence of the eye, not just a small eyeball.
Synophthalmia is the fusion of the eyes due to loss of midline structures.
Aphakia is the congenital absence of the lens, but the rest of the eyeball may be of normal size.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 488 (Book Page): In microphthalmia, the eye is too small; the eyeball may be only two-thirds of its normal volume. Usually associated with other ocular abnormalities, microphthalmia can result from intrauterine infections, such as cytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis.

category: Describe the development of face and nasolacrimal duct and their respective congenital anomalies
statement: What is the predominant embryological source of the mesenchyme that forms the facial prominences?
options: Neural crest cells
Sclerotome of the occipital somites
Surface ectoderm
Paraxial mesoderm
Lateral plate mesoderm
correctOption: Neural crest cells
optionExplanations: Neural crest cells migrate from the neural folds into the face to form the vast majority of the viscerocranium and facial connective tissues.
Sclerotome cells form the vertebrae and the chordal part of the skull base, not the mesenchymal prominences of the face.
Surface ectoderm provides the epithelial covering and specialized placodes of the face, but the internal bulk (mesenchyme) is derived from neural crest.
Paraxial mesoderm forms the skeletal muscles of the face and parts of the neurocranium, but the facial prominences themselves are primarily crest-derived.
Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to laryngeal cartilages but plays a minimal role in the formation of the facial prominences (maxillary, nasal, etc.).
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 420 (Book Page): facial prominences consisting primarily of neural crest-derived mesenchyme and formed mainly by the first pair of pharyngeal arches appear.

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: An infant is born with significant facial asymmetry, including a small, flat zygomatic bone and maxilla on the right side only, accompanied by preauricular skin tags and a hemivertebra in the cervical spine. Which condition best fits this asymmetrical presentation?
options: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome.
Treacher Collins Syndrome.
DiGeorge Syndrome.
Achondroplasia.
Goldenhar Syndrome (Hemifacial Microsomia).
correctOption: Goldenhar Syndrome (Hemifacial Microsomia).
optionExplanations: 22q11.2 Deletion syndrome is the broader category for DiGeorge; it is characterized by midline/symmetrical facial features and systemic glandular issues, not unilateral microsomia and hemivertebrae.
Treacher Collins syndrome is typically bilateral and symmetrical, involving hypoplasia of the zygomatic arches and mandible, without the specific vertebral defects of Goldenhar.
DiGeorge syndrome presents with symmetrical facial dysmorphology (small mouth, low set ears) and immune/cardiac defects rather than isolated hemi-facial hypoplasia.
Achondroplasia affects endochondral ossification leading to short limbs and megalocephaly but does not cause asymmetrical facial bone hypoplasia.

Goldenhar syndrome (hemifacial microsomia) is classically asymmetrical (65% of cases). It involves first and second arch derivatives plus vertebral anomalies like hemivertebrae (oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum).
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 416 (Book Page): Hemifacial microsomia [oculoauriculovertebral spectrum or Goldenhar syndrome]... Asymmetry is present in 65% of the cases... Ear [anotia, microtia], eye [tumors] and vertebral [fused and hemivertebrae] defects are commonly observed.

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: Thanatophoric dysplasia is the most common neonatal lethal form of skeletal dysplasia. Which molecular mechanism is responsible for the characteristic cloverleaf skull and severely shortened limbs found in Type II of this condition?
options: Mutations in the MSX2 gene affecting the coronal suture
Loss-of-function mutation in the EFNB1 ligand
Decreased mineralization of sutures due to RUNX2 deficiency
Mutations in the TWIST1 transcription factor
Gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 receptor
correctOption: Gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 receptor
optionExplanations: MSX2 mutations cause Boston-type craniosynostosis, which is not associated with the lethal skeletal defects of thanatophoric dysplasia.
Loss of function in EFNB1 causes craniofrontonasal syndrome, which features coronal synostosis and hypertelorism, not lethal dwarfism.
Decreased mineralization is a feature of cleidocranial dysostosis (RUNX2), which leads to open fontanelles rather than the premature fusion seen in thanatophoric dysplasia.
Mutations in TWIST1 cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, characterized by coronal synostosis and polydactyly, but not cloverleaf skull dwarfism.

FGFR3 normally inhibits chondrocyte proliferation. Constitutively active (gain-of-function) mutations lead to severe suppression of endochondral bone growth, causing short limbs and early fusion of all sutures.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): The shape of the skull results from abnormal growth of the cranial base, caused by a mutation in FGFR3, followed by craniosynostosis... Common to all of these forms of skeletal dysplasias are mutations in FGFR3.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
statement: During the 10th week of development, the cartilaginous shell surrounding the cochlear duct undergoes a specific morphological change to form the perilymphatic spaces. What is this mechanism?
options: Apoptosis of chondrocytes within the modiolus
Vacuolization of the cartilaginous shell
Dilation of the ductus reuniens
Expansion of the endolymphatic sac
Invagination of the surrounding neural crest cells
correctOption: Vacuolization of the cartilaginous shell
optionExplanations: The modiolus remains as a cartilaginous and then bony axis for the cochlea; its destruction would not create the scalae.
Correct. The scala vestibuli and scala tympani are created when the cartilaginous otic capsule undergoes vacuolization during the 10th week.
The ductus reuniens is a narrow connection between the saccule and cochlear duct, not involved in the formation of the scalae.
The endolymphatic sac is part of the endolymphatic (membranous) system, whereas the scalae contain perilymph.
Neural crest cells contribute to the ganglia and some ossicle parts but do not drive the formation of the perilymphatic spaces through invagination.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 472 (Book Page): In the 10th week, this cartilaginous shell undergoes vacuolization, and two perilymphatic spaces, the scala vestibuli and scala tympani, are formed.

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: A child presents with a distinctive appearance including a large head with bossing of the frontal and parietal bones, late closure of the fontanelles, and the unique ability to bring their shoulders together in the midline due to missing clavicles. Which condition is most likely?
options: Cleidocranial dysostosis
Microcephaly
Thanatophoric dysplasia Type II
Achondroplasia
Boston-type craniosynostosis
correctOption: Cleidocranial dysostosis
optionExplanations: Cleidocranial dysostosis is a systemic skeletal dysplasia specifically recognized by failed clavicular development and delayed ossification of skull sutures (bossing).
Microcephaly is characterized by a small head due to brain growth failure, whereas this child has an enlarged head (bossing).
Thanatophoric dysplasia Type II features a cloverleaf skull and severe limb shortening; it is usually lethal at birth and doesn't feature isolated clavicular absence.
Achondroplasia features short limbs and midfacial hypoplasia, but the clavicles are typically present and normal.
Boston-type craniosynostosis involves premature suture closure (craniosynostosis), which is the opposite of the delayed closure (late fontanelles) seen in dysostosis.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): Cleidocranial dysostosis is an example of a generalized dysplasia of osseus and dental tissues... oftentimes, the clavicles are underdeveloped or missing.

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: In a premature infant born at 28 weeks' gestation, the primary cause of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) is the high surface tension at the air-blood interface. Which cellular deficiency is directly responsible for this condition?
options: Lack of vacuum formation in the pleural cavity
Failure of the tracheoesophageal septum to form
Absence of type I alveolar epithelial cells
Inadequate production of surfactant by type II alveolar cells
Premature apoptosis of the visceral mesoderm
correctOption: Inadequate production of surfactant by type II alveolar cells
optionExplanations: Vacuum in the pleural cavity is maintained by the chest wall and diaphragm; while important for expansion, it is not the biochemical deficiency underlying RDS.
Failure of the tracheoesophageal septum results in fistulas/atresia, which affect swallowing and airway protection, but does not cause primary RDS due to surface tension.
Type I cells are the thin squamous cells that form the blood-air barrier. Their absence would prevent gas exchange, but RDS is specifically caused by the surface tension issues related to surfactant.
Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant starting at the end of the sixth month. Surfactant reduces surface tension; without it, alveoli collapse during expiration (atelectasis), leading to RDS.
Visceral mesoderm forms the supporting tissues and pleura; while necessary for lung structure, its 'apoptosis' is not a recognized mechanism for RDS.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 349 (Book Page): Absent or insufficient surfactant in the premature baby causes respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) because of collapse of the primitive alveoli (hyaline membrane disease). ... produced by type II alveolar epithelial cells

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Anatomy and Histogenesis of the Organ of Corti
statement: Regarding the transmission of sound, the tectorial membrane plays a critical role within the Organ of Corti. To which structure is this membrane embryologically and anatomically attached?
options: Spiral ligament
Vestibular membrane
Modiolus
Spiral limbus
Basilar membrane
correctOption: Spiral limbus
optionExplanations: The spiral ligament supports the lateral wall of the cochlear duct and does not serve as an attachment for the tectorial membrane.
The vestibular membrane forms the roof of the cochlear duct; it is not involved in the attachment of the tectorial membrane.
The modiolus is the central bony pillar of the cochlea; while it houses the spiral ganglion, it is not the direct attachment site for the tectorial membrane.
The tectorial membrane is attached to the spiral limbus (the derivative of the inner ridge of the cochlear duct) and extends over the hair cells.
The basilar membrane supports the hair cells, but the tectorial membrane is attached to the spiral limbus on the inner ridge side.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 472 (Book Page): They are covered by the tectorial membrane, a fibrillar gelatinous substance attached to the spiral limbus that rests with its tip on the hair cells (Fig. 19.5).

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
statement: In the transformation of the optic stalk into the optic nerve, what morphological change occurs as the nerve fibers converge from the retina?
options: The stalk invaginates to form the ciliary processes.
The outer wall of the stalk becomes the pigmented layer of the iris.
The hyaloid artery degenerates completely to leave a hollow nerve.
The inner and outer walls of the stalk fuse to obliterate the lumen.
The stalk detaches from the forebrain to become a peripheral nerve.
correctOption: The inner and outer walls of the stalk fuse to obliterate the lumen.
optionExplanations: Invagination to form ciliary processes occurs in the optic cup region (pars ciliaris retinae), not along the optic stalk.
The outer layer of the optic cup becomes the pigmented retina; the stalk walls specifically fuse to provide the neuroglial support for the nerve.
The hyaloid artery does not disappear from the nerve; its proximal portion persists as the central artery of the retina within the optic nerve.
As the number of axons from the ganglion cells increases, the walls of the optic stalk expand and eventually fuse, converting the stalk into a solid optic nerve.
The optic nerve remains a tract of the central nervous system and does not detach from the brain; it is surrounded by the three meningeal layers.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 485 (Book Page): As a result of the continuously increasing number of nerve fibers, the inner wall of the stalk grows, and the inside and outside walls of the stalk fuse.

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: A newborn is being evaluated for the VACTERL association. According to established diagnostic criteria for this collection of defects, which pair of anomalies must be investigated specifically regarding the development of the foregut?
options: Microcephaly and Holoprosencephaly
Tracheoesophageal fistula and Esophageal atresia
Renal anomalies and Radial dysplasia
Cardiac defects and Limb defects
Vertebral anomalies and Anal atresia
correctOption: Tracheoesophageal fistula and Esophageal atresia
optionExplanations: Microcephaly and holoprosencephaly are severe brain and skull defects but are not included in the standard VACTERL association criteria.
Tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) and Esophageal atresia (EA) are central components of VACTERL, resulting from the faulty partitioning of the foregut into the trachea and esophagus.
Renal anomalies are part of VACTERL, but radial/limb defects are categorized separately; neither represents the specific respiratory-esophageal foregut split.
These are the 'C' and 'L' of VACTERL but do not represent the developmental abnormalities of the tracheoesophageal septum.
While both are part of VACTERL (Vertebral and Anal), they are not the specific foregut partitioning defects described in the respiratory/esophageal section.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 345 (Book Page): In this regard, TEFs are a component of the VACTERL association [Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheoesophageal fistula, Esophageal atresia, Renal anomalies, and Limb defects].

category: List the components of pharyngeal apparatus
statement: At which specific point in embryonic development do the pharyngeal arches first begin to appear as bars of mesenchymal tissue?
options: Seventh and eighth weeks
Second and third weeks
Ninth and tenth weeks
Fourth and fifth weeks
End of the first trimester
correctOption: Fourth and fifth weeks
optionExplanations: Incorrect. By the 7th and 8th weeks, the arches have already begun differentiating into their definitive derivatives.
Incorrect. In the second and third weeks, gastrulation and early neurulation are occurring; the arches have not yet formed.
Incorrect. This is during the fetal period when the face is already formed.
Correct. Pharyngeal arches are a hallmark of the 4th and 5th weeks of human development.
Incorrect. The arches are embryonic structures that appear much earlier than the end of the first trimester.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 405 (Book Page): These arches appear in the fourth and fifth weeks of development and contribute to the characteristic external appearance of the embryo.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
statement: A 4-year-old child presents with moderate hearing loss. Otoscopic examination shows a blocked external auditory canal by a dense tissue mass. The physician suspects a failure in the normal developmental programmed cell death that occurs in the seventh month. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Absence of the ductus reuniens
Ankylosis of the stapes
Otic vesicle agenesis
Persistent meatal plug
Cochlear duct atresia
correctOption: Persistent meatal plug
optionExplanations: The ductus reuniens connects the saccule and cochlea internally; its absence would not block the external canal.
Ankylosis of the stapes is a middle ear defect involving ossification, not an epithelial mass in the external canal.
Otic vesicle agenesis would result in sensorineural deafness and absence of internal ear structures, not a mass in the external canal.
Correct. The meatal plug is a solid epithelial plate that should dissolve in the 7th month; its persistence causes conductive deafness.
Cochlear duct atresia is an internal ear defect and would not be visible in the external auditory canal.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 476 (Book Page): In the seventh month, this plug dissolves... Occasionally, the meatal plug persists until birth, resulting in congenital deafness.

category: Describe the development of larynx
statement: Which of the following components of the larynx is uniquely derived from the fourth pharyngeal arch mesenchyme and is innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve?
options: Cricoid cartilage
Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle
Cricothyroid muscle
True vocal cords
Thyroid gland
correctOption: Cricothyroid muscle
optionExplanations: The cricoid cartilage is derived from both the 4th and 6th arches, but the question asks for a component innervated by the nerve (a muscle).
The posterior cricoarytenoid is an intrinsic muscle supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (6th arch derivative).
The cricothyroid muscle is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle derived from the 4th arch and is thus innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve.
The vocal cords are tissue folds associated with the recanalization of the laryngeal lumen, rather than a specific arch muscle.
The thyroid gland is an endocrine organ that descends from the foramen cecum; it is not a muscle of the 4th arch.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 405 (Book Page): Table 17.1: Fourth arch... Nerve: Superior laryngeal branch... Muscles: Cricothyroid... Skeleton: Laryngeal cartilages.

category: Give the associated congenital anomalies
statement: If a pregnant woman is infected with the Rubella virus, the risk of her child developing congenital cataracts is highest if the infection occurs during which gestational period?
options: Weeks 8 to 12
Weeks 1 to 2
Weeks 13 to 20
Third trimester
Weeks 4 to 7
correctOption: Weeks 4 to 7
optionExplanations: By week 8, the primary lens fibers have filled the lumen of the lens vesicle, making the structure less susceptible to the specific cataractogenic effects of Rubella.
Weeks 1 to 2 represent the pre-embryonic phase where infection usually results in either death of the embryo or no effect (all-or-nothing).
Infection after the 7th week may result in other anomalies like hearing loss due to cochlear damage, but the lens is generally protected.
Rubella infection in the third trimester is associated with significantly lower risks of major structural congenital malformations like cataracts.
The lens vesicle forms and begins primary fiber elongation during the 4th to 7th weeks; interference during this specific window leads to lens opacification (cataracts).
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 487 (Book Page): many children born to mothers who had rubella [German measles] between the fourth and seventh weeks of pregnancy had cataracts. If the mother is infected after the seventh week of pregnancy, the lens escapes damage.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptors (FGFRs) play distinct roles in the regulation of bone development in the skull. According to current embryological understanding, what are the specific roles of FGFR1 and FGFR2 in suture regulation?
options: Both receptors have identical functions in promoting the synthesis of hyaline cartilage models.
FGFR1 promotes osteogenic differentiation, while FGFR2 increases proliferation.
FGFR1 prevents suture closure, while FGFR2 stimulates apoptosis of chondrocytes.
FGFR1 regulates neural crest migration, while FGFR2 regulates paraxial mesoderm migration.
FGFR1 increases cell proliferation, while FGFR2 promotes osteogenic differentiation.
correctOption: FGFR1 promotes osteogenic differentiation, while FGFR2 increases proliferation.
optionExplanations: The functions are distinct; the flat bones of the skull vault (membranous) do not even utilize a hyaline cartilage model, as they undergo intramembranous ossification.

In the complex signaling of the cranial sutures, FGFR2 is responsible for increasing the number of precursor cells (proliferation), and FGFR1 signals these cells to differentiate into bone-forming cells (osteogenesis).
While these receptors regulate closure, the specific mechanism described in the text is the balance between proliferation and differentiation, not direct apoptosis regulation.
Migration is largely regulated by other factors like BMPs and Wnt; FGFR1 and FGFR2 are more involved in the subsequent differentiation and growth phases.
This option reverses the roles; FGFR2 is the one that typically drives the proliferative phase of the pre-bone cells.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): In general, FGFR2 increases proliferation, and FGFR1 promotes osteogenic differentiation, whereas the role of FGFR3 is unclear.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: During a routine neonatal examination, a house officer palpates the anterior fontanelle. According to standard embryological timelines, by what age should this fontanelle typically be closed?
options: 24 months
12 months
18 months
3 months
6 months
correctOption: 18 months
optionExplanations: Closure by 24 months is slightly late; the second year is when closure finishes, specifically around the 18-month mark.
While some children's fontanelles may close at 12 months, the standard developmental expectation is 18 months.
The anterior fontanelle, located at the junction of the sagittal, coronal, and frontal sutures, typically closes around 18 months of age.
The posterior fontanelle usually closes around this time (1-3 months), but the anterior fontanelle remains open much longer.
Six months is too early for anterior fontanelle closure; early closure may suggest craniosynostosis.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 270 (Book Page): In most cases, the anterior fontanelle closes by 18 months of age, and the posterior fontanelle closes by 1 to 2 months of age.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
statement: Molecular signaling is crucial for the regionalization of the optic cup. Which gene is considered the master regulator of eye development and is expressed in the optic cup and lens-forming surface ectoderm?
options: PAX2
CHX10
SHH
PAX6
MITF
correctOption: PAX6
optionExplanations: PAX2 is upregulated by SHH in the midline and is specifically expressed in the optic stalks, not the cup and lens.
CHX10 is a transcription factor specific for the differentiation of the neural layer of the retina.
Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) is responsible for separating the eye field into two optic primordia by inhibiting PAX6 in the midline.
PAX6 is the master control gene for the eye; it establishes the eye field and regulates the differentiation of the lens and optic cup.
MITF is a transcription factor specific for the differentiation of the pigmented layer of the retina.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 485 (Book Page): PAX6 is the key regulatory gene for eye development. ... it appears that PAX6 is not essential for optic cup formation. ... Instead, PAX6 acts in the surface ectoderm to regulate lens development.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
statement: A 55-year-old patient is diagnosed with glaucoma. Embryologically, this condition is often related to the improper drainage of aqueous humor. Through which structure, located at the iridocorneal angle, does the aqueous humor normally exit the anterior chamber to enter the bloodstream?
options: Suspensory ligament of the lens
Vitreous body
Hyaloid canal
Ciliary process
Scleral venous sinus (Canal of Schlemm)
correctOption: Scleral venous sinus (Canal of Schlemm)
optionExplanations: The suspensory ligament (zonules) holds the lens in place and transmits the pull of the ciliary muscle; it has no role in fluid drainage.
The vitreous body is the gelatinous substance in the posterior chamber; while it contains fluid, it is not part of the active drainage pathway for aqueous humor.
The hyaloid canal is a remnant of the hyaloid artery pathway in the vitreous body and does not participate in anterior chamber fluid dynamics.
The ciliary process is the site of production of the aqueous humor, not its drainage.
The Canal of Schlemm is the physiological drain for aqueous humor. Embryologically, it forms at the junction of the developing cornea and sclera (the limbus).
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 484 (Book Page): From the anterior chamber, the fluid passes through the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm) at the iridocorneal angle where it is resorbed into the bloodstream. Blockage of the flow of fluid at the canal of Schlemm is one cause of glaucoma.

category: Describe the development of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses
statement: During the sixth week of development, the nasal pits deepen and penetrate the underlying mesenchyme. What specific structure initially separates these primitive nasal cavities from the oral cavity?
options: Oronasal membrane
Intermaxillary segment
Primary palate
Secondary palate
Nasolacrimal groove
correctOption: Oronasal membrane
optionExplanations: The oronasal membrane is a transient epithelial structure that separates the deepening nasal pits from the primitive oral cavity until it breaks down to establish the primitive choanae.
The intermaxillary segment is a deeper tissue mass formed by merged medial nasal prominences; while it contains the primary palate, it is a tissue volume rather than the separating membrane.

The primary palate is a structural component of the intermaxillary segment that forms the anterior-most portion of the roof of the mouth, but it does not serve as the initial temporary membrane between the cavities.
The secondary palate forms later (starting in the 6th-7th week) from palatine shelves and eventually provides the definitive separation, but it is not the initial barrier.
The nasolacrimal groove is a furrow between the maxillary and lateral nasal prominences that develops into the nasolacrimal duct; it does not separate the oral and nasal cavities.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 422 (Book Page): At first, the oronasal membrane separates the pits from the primitive oral cavity by way of the newly formed foramina, the primitive choanae.

category: Describe the development of face and nasolacrimal duct and their respective congenital anomalies
statement: Upon successful canalization and development, the nasolacrimal duct ultimately terminates and drains into which anatomical location?
options: The superior meatus of the nasal cavity
The middle meatus of the nasal cavity
The inferior meatus of the nasal cavity
The nasopharynx posterior to the choanae
The vestibule of the oral cavity
correctOption: The inferior meatus of the nasal cavity
optionExplanations: The superior meatus receives drainage from the posterior ethmoidal air cells, not the nasolacrimal duct.
The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses.
The nasolacrimal duct specifically drains into the inferior meatus, located beneath the inferior nasal concha.
The nasopharynx is the area posterior to the nasal cavity; the duct terminates within the nasal cavity proper at the inferior meatus.
The oral cavity is separated from the nasal cavity by the palate; the duct does not enter the oral space.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 420 (Book Page): The nasolacrimal duct then runs from the medial corner of the eye to the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity, and the maxillary prominences enlarge to form the cheeks and maxillae.

category: Describe the development and histogenesis of auditory tube, tympanic cavity, tonsils, thymus and parathyroid
statement: What is the typical fate of the thymus gland in older adults?
options: It expands to fill the entire anterior mediastinum.
It is atrophied and replaced by fatty tissue.
It migrates back to the neck region.
It becomes the primary site of calcitonin production.
It undergoes malignant transformation into a thymoma.
correctOption: It is atrophied and replaced by fatty tissue.
optionExplanations: The thymus is large in children, but it shrinks (involutes) in adults rather than expanding.
Correct. After puberty, the thymus undergoes atrophy and is largely replaced by fat (adipose tissue).
The thymus does not migrate back; its descent is a one-way process during embryogenesis.
Calcitonin is produced by the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland, not the thymus.
Thymoma is a pathology, but the physiological fate of the thymus is involution/atrophy, not cancer.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 411 (Book Page): Growth and development of the thymus continue until puberty. In the young child, the thymus occupies considerable space in the thorax... In older persons, it is difficult to recognize because it is atrophied and replaced by fatty tissue.

category: Describe the development of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses
statement: Clinical assessment of facial proportions changes significantly during childhood. At what stage of human development do the paranasal air sinuses reach their maximum size?
options: At the end of the seventh month of gestation
During the eruption of deciduous teeth
At approximately 5 years of age
Immediately at birth
During puberty
correctOption: During puberty
optionExplanations: At seven months gestation, the sinuses are only just beginning to form or are very small; they do not reach full size in utero.
The eruption of deciduous teeth (6-24 months) contributes to jaw growth, but the sinuses continue to expand long after this stage.
While a child has significant cranial capacity by age 5-7, the facial skeleton and sinuses continue to develop through adolescence until puberty.
In newborns, the face is small compared to the neurocranium partly because the paranasal sinuses are virtually absent or very small.
The paranasal sinuses undergo significant expansion postnatally and only reach their maximum dimensions during puberty, coinciding with secondary facial growth.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 422 (Book Page): They reach their maximum size during puberty and contribute to the definitive shape of the face.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: The molecular regulation of suture growth involves interactions between neural crest cells and paraxial mesoderm. Which ligand-receptor system is specifically noted for providing anti-adhesive activity to prevent the premature fusion of these mesenchymal boundaries?
options: FGF1 and FGFR2.
MSX2 and TWIST1.
SHH and Patched receptors.
BMP4 and Noggin.
EFNB1 and EphB receptors.
correctOption: EFNB1 and EphB receptors.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. FGF1 and FGFR2 are involved in osteogenic differentiation and proliferation, often promoting bone formation rather than preventing it via anti-adhesion.
Incorrect. MSX2 and TWIST1 are transcription factors that regulate neural crest cell proliferation in the frontal bones.
Incorrect. Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is vital for midline establishment and limb patterning, but is not the primary anti-adhesive regulator in cranial sutures cited.
Incorrect. BMP4 is involved in bone induction and apoptosis, but it is not described as the specific anti-adhesive mechanism for suture maintenance.
Correct. The ephrin-B1 (EFNB1) and EphB receptor system mediates cell repulsion (anti-adhesion), which keeps the sutures open; loss of this results in craniofrontonasal syndrome.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): For example, EFNB1 encodes ephrin-B1, a ligand for EphB receptors that causes cells to repel each other, a kind of antiadhesive activity and important for preventing premature suture closure.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
statement: Which developmental mechanism explains why light must pass through the ganglion and nuclear layers of the retina before reaching the photoreceptive rods and cones in the human eye?
options: The pigmented layer of the retina develops from the inner wall of the optic cup.
The hyaloid artery supplies the neural retina from the external surface only.
The rods and cones differentiate from the layer bordering the obliterated intraretinal space.
The lens vesicle invaginates from the inner layer of the optic cup.
The optic stalk originates from the surface ectoderm rather than the forebrain.
correctOption: The rods and cones differentiate from the layer bordering the obliterated intraretinal space.
optionExplanations: The pigmented layer develops from the outer wall of the optic cup, not the inner wall.
The vascular supply does not dictate the orientation of the photoreceptors; the orientation is due to the invagination of the optic vesicle to form the cup.

Correct. Because the rods and cones develop from the deepest cells of the inner layer (adjacent to the intraretinal space), they are at the back of the neural retina, requiring light to pass through the more superficial layers.
The lens vesicle develops from surface ectoderm, not the optic cup, and its location does not explain the internal layering of the retina.
The optic stalk originates from the neuroectoderm of the forebrain, not the surface ectoderm.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 482 (Book Page): The posterior four-fifths, the pars optica retinae, contains cells bordering the intraretinal space (Fig. 20.3) that differentiate into the photoreceptive rods and cones... Hence, light impulses pass through most layers of the retina before they reach the rods and cones.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Morphogenesis of the Semicircular Canals and Crura
statement: Regarding the morphogenesis of the semicircular canals, how is the 'crus commune nonampullare' specifically formed within the internal ear?
options: By the failure of the central wall portions to appose and disappear
As a direct outgrowth from the ventral saccular portion
Through the individual dilation of the posterior semicircular canal
Through the fusion of the non-widened ends of two semicircular canals
From the invagination of the first pharyngeal arch tissue
correctOption: Through the fusion of the non-widened ends of two semicircular canals
optionExplanations: The disappearance of the central wall portions is the process that forms the canals themselves, but the crus commune nonampullare refers to the junction where they enter the utricle.
The semicircular canals and their crura are derivatives of the dorsal utricular portion, not the ventral saccular portion.
The crus ampullare is the dilated end of a canal; the crus commune nonampullare is specifically the fused, non-widened ends.
The crus commune nonampullare is formed when the two non-widened ends (crus nonampullare) of the superior and posterior canals fuse, resulting in a single opening into the utricle.
Invagination of the first pharyngeal arch tissue forms the external auditory meatus, not the internal semicircular canals.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 474 (Book Page): Whereas, one end of each canal dilates to form the crus ampullare, the other, the crus nonampullare, does not widen (Fig. 19.6). Because two of the latter type fuse, however, only five crura enter the utricle, three with an ampulla and two without.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
statement: Which of the following describes a rare congenital anomaly characterized by the complete absence of the iris, often resulting from mutations in the master eye gene PAX6?
options: Aphakia
Aniridia
Cyclopia
Microphthalmia
Coloboma iridis
correctOption: Aniridia
optionExplanations: Aphakia is the congenital absence of the lens, not the iris.
Correct. Aniridia is the absence of the iris, specifically linked in the text to mutations in the PAX6 gene.
Cyclopia is the presence of a single midline eye, which is a midline separation defect, not specifically an iris absence defect.
Microphthalmia refers to an abnormally small eye, often two-thirds of normal volume, rather than the specific absence of the iris.
Coloboma iridis is a cleft in the iris due to failure of the choroid fissure to close, but the iris itself is present, albeit with a defect.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 488 (Book Page): Congenital aphakia [absence of the lens] and aniridia [absence of the iris; Fig. 20.11] are rare anomalies... Mutations in PAX6 result in aniridia.

category: Discuss the embryological basis of congenital anomalies related to the development of pharyngeal arches, pharyngeal clefts and pharyngeal pouches: cervical sinus/fistula/cyst, 1st arch syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome, congenital malformations of thymus and parathyroid glands
statement: During the fifth week of development, the second pharyngeal arch grows caudally and overlaps the third and fourth arches. What is the typical developmental fate of the resulting ectoderm-lined cervical sinus?
options: It gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands
It forms the epithelial lining of the external auditory meatus
It is normally obliterated and disappears
It differentiates into the palatine tonsil stroma
It becomes the thyroglossal duct
correctOption: It is normally obliterated and disappears
optionExplanations: The inferior parathyroid glands arise from the dorsal wing of the third pharyngeal pouch (endoderm), not the ectodermal cervical sinus.
The external auditory meatus is formed by the invagination of surface ectoderm from the first pharyngeal arch, not the cervical sinus (which involves clefts 2, 3, and 4).
The cervical sinus is a temporary space formed by the overgrowth of the second arch. In normal development, it is completely obliterated. Persistence leads to branchial cysts or fistulas.
The palatine tonsil stroma is derived from the second pharyngeal pouch (endoderm), not the ectodermal cervical sinus.
The thyroglossal duct is a midline structure formed by the descent of the thyroid primordium from the foramen cecum, unrelated to the lateral cervical sinus.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 411 (Book Page): The clefts form a cavity lined with ectodermal epithelium, the cervical sinus, but with further development, this sinus disappears.

category: Describe the development of Skull
statement: A 3-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic due to an abnormal head shape. On examination, the head is notably long and narrow (scaphocephaly), with a palpable ridge along the midline. The mother reports that the 'soft spot' on the back of the head closed very early. Which suture is most likely involved in this premature closure?
options: Coronal suture
Metopic suture
Squamosal suture
Sagittal suture
Lambdoid suture
correctOption: Sagittal suture
optionExplanations: Premature closure of the coronal sutures (brachycephaly) results in a short, wide skull, not a long, narrow one.
The metopic (frontal) suture closure can lead to trigonocephaly (triangular forehead), which is not described here.
The squamosal suture is located between the parietal and temporal bones; its isolated premature closure is rare and does not result in the scaphocephalic phenotype.
Sagittal suture synostosis prevents lateral growth of the skull, forcing expansion anteriorly and posteriorly, resulting in a long, narrow head (scaphocephaly).
Closure of the lambdoid suture is less common and typically contributes to posterior plagiocephaly if unilateral; it does not produce the classic scaphocephalic shape.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 272 (Book Page): Early closure of the sagittal suture [57% of cases] results in frontal and occipital expansion, and the skull becomes long and narrow [scaphocephaly].

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Tonotopic Mapping of the Basilar Membrane
statement: In the physiological development of the cochlea, which anatomical arrangement allows for the perception of high-frequency (high pitch) sound waves near the oval window?
options: The presence of longer, more flexible fibers in the basilar membrane
The resonance of the tectorial membrane in the scala tympani
The proximity to the ductus reuniens and the saccule
The specific density of the spiral limbus at the cochlear apex
The attachment of shorter, stiffer fibers to the basilar membrane
correctOption: The attachment of shorter, stiffer fibers to the basilar membrane
optionExplanations: Longer, more flexible fibers are found farther up the cochlea and resonate with lower frequency waves.
Resonance occurs in the basilar membrane fibers, not the tectorial membrane, and it happens in the cochlear duct (scala media).
Proximity to the saccule via the ductus reuniens does not determine frequency localization; this is a property of the basilar membrane's physical characteristics.
The spiral limbus provides attachment for the tectorial membrane but does not dictate the frequency resonance of the cochlea; that is the role of the basilar membrane fibers.
The basilar membrane has shorter, stiffer fibers near the oval window, which makes this region responsive to high-frequency sound waves.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 477 (Book Page): High frequencies (high pitch) are heard near the oval window where fibers connecting the basilar membrane are shorter and stiffer; lower frequencies are heard farther up the cochlea where the fibers are longer and more flexible.

category: List the components of pharyngeal apparatus
statement: Which specific arterial structure is a mandatory component found within the mesenchymal core of every pharyngeal arch?
options: Hyaloid artery
Aortic arch artery
Internal carotid artery
External carotid artery
Stapedial artery
correctOption: Aortic arch artery
optionExplanations: The hyaloid artery is a vessel of the developing eye, reaching the inner chamber through the choroid fissure, not a component of the pharyngeal arches.
Each of the pharyngeal arches (1, 2, 3, 4, 6) contains its own aortic arch artery that arises from the aortic sac.
The internal carotid is a derivative specifically associated with the third aortic arch, not a component of every arch.
The external carotid arises as a sprout from the aortic arch system but is not the primary arterial component within the primitive arches.
The stapedial artery is the specific arterial component of the second pharyngeal arch; it is not found in all arches.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 406 (Book Page): Each pharyngeal arch consists of a core of mesenchymal tissue... each arch has its own arterial component (Figs. 17.4 and 17.6). ... (Fig 17.6 caption): Each arch also contains an artery [one of the aortic arches] and a cranial nerve.

category: List the components of pharyngeal apparatus
statement: Which skeletal element is exclusively derived from the cartilaginous component of the third pharyngeal arch?
options: The lesser horn and upper body of the hyoid bone
The greater horn and lower body of the hyoid bone
The thyroid and cricoid cartilages
The malleus and incus
The stapes and styloid process
correctOption: The greater horn and lower body of the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The lesser horn and upper part of the body of the hyoid are derived from the second arch, not the third.
